artifacts.response:
Winter Storm Uri struck Texas in February 2021, arriving over the weekend of February 13 and 14, and it was only after its arrival that ERCOT ordered rotating outages beginning on February 15, 2021. The sequence was fast. In the early hours of that Monday, as generating units tripped offline faster than operators could compensate, ERCOT's grid frequency fell below 59.4 hertz for more than four minutes. Sustained operation at that level would have triggered automatic protective disconnection of generation. Either the ERCOT grid avoided an uncontrolled total blackout during the February 2021 storm, or it suffered one; there was no intermediate outcome, and the record establishes the first. ERCOT's peak load shed during the storm reached roughly 20,000 megawatts, and that scale of controlled curtailment indicates how the system was held together: operators removed demand deliberately so that the remaining generation could stabilize frequency.

Attributing the shortfall required a different body of evidence than the operational logs that described the frequency event. FERC and NERC conducted a joint inquiry into the February 2021 grid event, assembling unit-by-unit outage data from generator owners, fuel suppliers, and balancing authorities. From that dataset the inquiry determined that freezing-related issues were the leading cause of unplanned generator outages during the storm. The gas system was exposed on two fronts. At least one of two failures cut gas-fired output at any given plant, and in many cases both did. Frozen gas wellheads and gathering lines reduced fuel supply to Texas power plants. In other cases the failure was on site: frozen instrumentation and equipment at gas-fired plants forced generating units offline. This on-site failure is a specific instance of the freezing problem the inquiry ranked first, since sensing lines, transmitters, and valves without adequate heat tracing or enclosure lost function at subfreezing temperatures. Because those component failures struck the most numerous class of dispatchable plants, natural gas-fired units made up the largest share of unplanned generation outages. In other words, no fuel type accounted for more unplanned generation outages than natural gas.

The question of wind generation was resolved with the same tallies rather than with anecdote. Some wind turbines in Texas froze during the storm, and photographs of iced blades circulated widely in the days that followed. Although those freezes were real, the FERC-NERC final report found that wind turbines accounted for only a modest fraction of unplanned generation outages. The report also observed that ERCOT's winter planning assumptions had already projected low wind output, so lost wind production fell against a smaller expected baseline. The dominance of gas-fired units in the outage counts provides the evidence behind the report's central attribution. The FERC-NERC final report concluded that natural gas generation was a far larger contributor to the outages than wind generation, and that conclusion settles the tension between the visible frozen turbines and the actual distribution of lost capacity.

The method that produced this answer was comparative. Investigators classified each unplanned outage, derate, or failure to start by fuel type and by proximate cause. They then weighted those events by megawatts lost and by duration. They did not rely on whichever failure was most visible or most politically salient. That approach distinguished equipment freezing at the plant from fuel curtailment upstream, and it showed that the two mechanisms compounded each other in the gas sector. It also placed wind outages in proportion. Because the work rested on a common outage dataset, state reviewers at the Public Utility Commission and in the Texas Legislature were working from the same numbers as the federal inquiry. Their subsequent weatherization mandates for generators and for critical gas facilities followed from those findings.

Their subsequent weatherization mandates for generators and for critical gas facilities followed from those findings.
